title: Types of APIs Explained Simply
intro: APIs are the backbone of modern applications. They help different software systems communicate and share data seamlessly.

slides.heading: REST API
slides.subtitle: The most widely used API type.
points: Uses HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
Lightweight and easy to use
Returns data mostly in JSON format

slides.heading: SOAP API
slides.subtitle: A protocol for secure, structured communication.
points: Uses XML format for messages
Highly secure with built-in error handling
Common in enterprise applications

slides.heading: GraphQL API
slides.subtitle: Ask for exactly the data you need.
points: Single endpoint for all queries
Client decides the response shape
Avoids over-fetching and under-fetching

slides.heading: WebSocket API
slides.subtitle: Two-way communication that stays open.
points: Persistent connection between client and server
Server can push data without a new request
Much lower latency than polling

slides.heading: gRPC API
slides.subtitle: Fast, typed communication between services.
points: Uses Protocol Buffers, not JSON
Much faster than REST for service-to-service calls
Strict, strongly-typed contracts

cta: Which API have you used the most? Let me know in the comments.

title: HTTP Status Codes You Must Know
intro: Every API response carries a status code. Knowing what they mean saves hours of debugging.

slides.heading: 2xx Success
slides.subtitle: The request worked as expected.
points: 200 OK — standard successful response
201 Created — a new resource was made
204 No Content — success, nothing to return

slides.heading: 3xx Redirection
slides.subtitle: The resource moved somewhere else.
points: 301 Moved Permanently — update your bookmarks
302 Found — temporary redirect
304 Not Modified — use your cached copy

slides.heading: 4xx Client Error
slides.subtitle: The request itself was the problem.
points: 400 Bad Request — malformed input
401 Unauthorized — you're not logged in
403 Forbidden — logged in, but not allowed
404 Not Found — the resource doesn't exist

slides.heading: 5xx Server Error
slides.subtitle: The request was fine, the server wasn't.
points: 500 Internal Server Error — something crashed
502 Bad Gateway — upstream server failed
503 Service Unavailable — server is overloaded

cta: Which status code do you see the most in your logs?

title: SQL JOINs Explained Simply
intro: JOINs combine rows from two or more tables. Pick the wrong one and you either lose data or duplicate it.

slides.heading: INNER JOIN
slides.subtitle: Only rows that match in both tables.
points: Returns rows where the join condition is true in both tables
Rows with no match on either side are excluded
The most commonly used join
examples: Orders that have a matching customer

slides.heading: LEFT JOIN
slides.subtitle: Everything from the left table, matched or not.
points: Keeps all rows from the left table
Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL
Useful for finding what's missing
examples: All customers, even those with zero orders

slides.heading: RIGHT JOIN
slides.subtitle: The mirror image of LEFT JOIN.
points: Keeps all rows from the right table
Unmatched left-side columns come back as NULL
Rarely used — most people rewrite it as a LEFT JOIN
examples: All products, even unordered ones, from the orders table

slides.heading: FULL JOIN
slides.subtitle: Everything from both tables.
points: Combines LEFT and RIGHT JOIN results
Unmatched rows from either side get NULLs
Good for finding mismatches between two tables
examples: Reconciling two systems that should be in sync

title: Git Commands Every Developer Needs
intro: You don't need 100 git commands memorized. These cover 90% of daily work.

slides.heading: Starting out
slides.subtitle: Get a project under version control.
points: git init — start tracking a new project
git clone <url> — copy an existing repo
git status — see what's changed

slides.heading: Saving work
slides.subtitle: Record changes as commits.
points: git add <file> — stage a change
git commit -m "message" — save staged changes
git push — send commits to the remote

slides.heading: Branching
slides.subtitle: Work on features without breaking main.
points: git switch -c <name> — create and move to a new branch
git switch <name> — move to an existing branch
git merge <name> — bring a branch's changes in

slides.heading: Undoing things
slides.subtitle: Mistakes happen, git can fix most of them.
points: git restore <file> — discard uncommitted changes
git reset --soft HEAD~1 — undo last commit, keep changes
git revert <commit> — safely undo a pushed commit

title: Web Security Basics Every Dev Should Know
intro: Most breaches don't come from genius hackers — they come from skipped basics. Start here.

slides.heading: SQL Injection
slides.subtitle: Untrusted input treated as executable SQL.
points: Happens when queries are built with string concatenation
An attacker can read or delete your entire database
Fixed with parameterized queries, never string building

slides.heading: XSS
slides.subtitle: Malicious scripts injected into your pages.
points: Happens when user input is rendered as raw HTML
Can steal cookies, sessions, and user data
Fixed by escaping output and using a strict CSP

slides.heading: CSRF
slides.subtitle: Tricking a logged-in user into an unwanted action.
points: Exploits the browser automatically sending cookies
Victim's own session is used against them
Fixed with CSRF tokens and SameSite cookies

slides.heading: Broken Auth
slides.subtitle: Weaknesses in login and session handling.
points: Weak password rules make brute-forcing easy
Tokens that never expire stay valid forever if leaked
Fixed with rate limiting, hashing, and short-lived tokens

cta: Which of these have you actually seen in production code?

title: How Caching Actually Works
intro: Caching is the single biggest lever for making an app feel fast. Here's how it's layered in a real system.

slides.heading: Browser Cache
slides.subtitle: The data never leaves the user's device.
points: Controlled by Cache-Control and ETag headers
Fastest possible response: zero network time
Best for static assets like images, CSS, JS

slides.heading: CDN Cache
slides.subtitle: A copy stored close to the user.
points: Edge servers around the world cache responses
Cuts latency by avoiding your origin server entirely
Great for content that's the same for every user

slides.heading: Application Cache
slides.subtitle: In-memory store like Redis sitting in front of your database.
points: Much faster than querying the database every time
Needs an invalidation strategy or data goes stale
Usually has a TTL as a safety net

slides.heading: Database Cache
slides.subtitle: The database's own internal optimizations.
points: Query plans and recently read pages are kept in memory
You don't control it directly, but indexes help it a lot
Still the slowest layer in this whole chain
examples: Hot rows in a popular table

cta: Which caching layer do you rely on most in your stack?

title: The JavaScript Event Loop, Simply
intro: JavaScript is single-threaded, yet handles thousands of operations without freezing. This is how.

slides.heading: Call Stack
slides.subtitle: Where your code actually executes.
points: Functions are pushed on when called, popped off when done
Only one thing runs at a time here
A long-running function here blocks everything else

slides.heading: Web APIs
slides.subtitle: Where async work actually happens.
points: Timers, network requests and DOM events run outside the stack
Provided by the browser or Node, not JS itself
They report back once finished, not immediately

slides.heading: Microtask Queue
slides.subtitle: The high-priority line for promises.
points: Holds resolved Promise callbacks and queueMicrotask
Always fully drained before the next macrotask runs
This is why a resolved promise logs before a timer

slides.heading: Macrotask Queue
slides.subtitle: Where the next 'turn' of work waits.
points: Holds timers, I/O callbacks, and UI events
Only one macrotask runs per loop iteration
Runs only after the stack and microtasks are empty

cta: Did you know microtasks always run before the next timer?

title: Code Review Habits That Make You Look Senior
intro: The difference between a junior and senior PR often isn't the code — it's these habits.

slides.heading: Self-review first
slides.subtitle: Read your own diff before requesting review.
points: Catches typos and leftover console.logs
Lets you add context comments on tricky parts
Shows reviewers you respect their time

slides.heading: Small PRs
slides.subtitle: Easier to review means faster to merge.
points: Split unrelated changes into separate PRs
A 100-line PR gets reviewed same-day, a 1000-line one doesn't
Smaller diffs mean fewer missed bugs

slides.heading: Clear descriptions
slides.subtitle: Explain the why, not just the what.
points: Link the ticket or issue being solved
Mention tradeoffs you considered and rejected
Add a test plan so reviewers know how to verify it
examples: PR template with context + test plan

slides.heading: Respond fast
slides.subtitle: Momentum matters more than perfection.
points: Reply to review comments within a day, not a week
Disagree directly in comments, don't go silent
Thank reviewers for catching real issues
examples: Addressing comments same day they're posted

title: Your Beginner's Roadmap to Web Development
intro: Don't know where to start? Follow these five steps in order and you'll go from zero to a live website you can show people.

slides.heading: 1. HTML & CSS
slides.subtitle: Structure and style every web page.
points: HTML gives a page its structure: headings, links, forms
CSS controls layout, colors and fonts
Learn Flexbox and Grid for layouts

slides.heading: 2. JavaScript
slides.subtitle: Make your pages interactive.
points: Variables, functions, arrays and objects
Handling clicks and updating the page (the DOM)
Loading data from APIs with fetch()

slides.heading: 3. Git & GitHub
slides.subtitle: Track your code and show your work.
points: Commit often with clear messages
Push every project to GitHub
Learn branches early, not later

slides.heading: 4. One Framework
slides.subtitle: Pick one and go deep.
points: React is a common, job-friendly choice
Learn components, props and state
Avoid hopping between frameworks early

slides.heading: 5. Deploy It
slides.subtitle: Put your projects online.
points: Vercel, Netlify and GitHub Pages offer free tiers
A live link beats a screenshot
Add a README explaining what you built
examples: Sharing a link in your resume

title: Frontend vs Backend vs Full Stack
intro: Three job titles you'll see everywhere. Here's what each one actually does, in plain language.

slides.heading: Frontend
slides.subtitle: Everything the user sees and touches.
points: Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript
Frameworks like React, Vue or Angular
Cares about UI, accessibility and speed

slides.heading: Backend
slides.subtitle: The logic and data behind the scenes.
points: Built with Node.js, Python, Java, Go and more
Handles databases, APIs and login
Cares about security and reliability

slides.heading: Full Stack
slides.subtitle: Comfortable on both sides.
points: Builds features end to end
Broad skills, usually deeper on one side
Common in startups and small teams

slides.heading: Which to pick?
slides.subtitle: Start where the work feels fun.
points: Love visuals and design? Try frontend
Love logic and data? Try backend
You can always switch later

cta: Frontend, backend or full stack: which one are you?

title: CSS Flexbox vs Grid, Explained Simply
intro: Both are for layout, but they solve different problems. Knowing which to reach for saves a lot of frustration.

slides.heading: Flexbox
slides.subtitle: Layout in one direction: a row or a column.
points: Add display: flex to the parent
justify-content aligns along the main axis
align-items aligns along the cross axis

slides.heading: Grid
slides.subtitle: Layout in two directions: rows and columns.
points: Add display: grid to the parent
grid-template-columns defines the columns
gap adds space between items

slides.heading: When to use which
slides.subtitle: A simple rule of thumb.
points: Items in a single line? Use Flexbox
Rows and columns together? Use Grid
They work great combined
examples: Grid for the page, Flexbox inside each card

slides.heading: Centering, solved
slides.subtitle: The classic beginner question.
points: Flexbox: justify-content and align-items: center
Grid: place-items: center
Both center horizontally and vertically

cta: Team Flexbox or team Grid?

title: Async JavaScript: Callbacks, Promises, async/await
intro: Async code lets JavaScript wait for slow things, like network requests, without freezing the page.

slides.heading: Callbacks
slides.subtitle: Pass a function to run later.
points: The original way to handle async work
Deep nesting leads to "callback hell"
Error handling gets messy fast

slides.heading: Promises
slides.subtitle: An object for a value that arrives later.
points: States: pending, fulfilled or rejected
Chain with .then() and .catch()
Promise.all runs tasks in parallel

slides.heading: async / await
slides.subtitle: Promise code that reads like normal code.
points: async functions always return a Promise
await pauses until the Promise settles
Use try/catch to handle errors

slides.heading: Common mistakes
slides.subtitle: Bugs almost everyone hits once.
points: Forgetting await and getting a Promise back
Awaiting independent calls one by one
No .catch() or try/catch for failures

cta: Which one clicked for you first: promises or async/await?

title: Authentication vs Authorization
intro: They sound alike but answer two different questions. Mixing them up is a common source of security bugs.

slides.heading: Authentication
slides.subtitle: Who are you?
points: Verifies a user's identity
Passwords, one-time codes, passkeys or social login
Always happens before authorization

slides.heading: Authorization
slides.subtitle: What are you allowed to do?
points: Checks permissions after login
Often role-based: admin, editor, viewer
Must be enforced on the server

slides.heading: Sessions
slides.subtitle: The server remembers who you are.
points: Server stores the session, browser keeps an ID cookie
Easy to log a user out by deleting the session
Classic choice for server-rendered apps

slides.heading: JWT
slides.subtitle: A signed token the client carries.
points: Holds user info signed by the server
Can be verified without a database lookup
Hard to revoke, so keep expiry short

cta: Do you prefer sessions or JWTs in your projects?

title: Big O Notation Explained Simply
intro: Big O describes how your code slows down as the input grows. It's the language every coding interview uses.

slides.heading: What is Big O?
slides.subtitle: How work grows as input grows.
points: Describes how time or memory scales
Ignores constants, focuses on growth
Usually describes the worst case
examples: Comparing two ways to solve a problem

slides.heading: O(1) Constant
slides.subtitle: Same time no matter the size.
points: Reading an array item by its index
Looking up a key in a hash map (on average)

slides.heading: O(n) Linear
slides.subtitle: Work grows with the input.
points: Looping through every item once
Double the input, roughly double the time
examples: Finding the max in an array

slides.heading: O(log n)
slides.subtitle: Halve the problem at every step.
points: Binary search on a sorted array
1 million items takes about 20 steps

slides.heading: O(n²) Quadratic
slides.subtitle: Nested loops over the same data.
points: Compares every item with every other item
Gets slow quickly on large inputs
Often fixable with a hash map

title: Docker Basics Every Developer Should Know
intro: Docker packages your app with everything it needs, so it runs the same on every machine.

slides.heading: What is Docker?
slides.subtitle: Apps in portable, isolated boxes.
points: Runs apps in isolated containers
Same environment on every machine
Ends "it works on my machine"

slides.heading: Image vs Container
slides.subtitle: The recipe vs the running dish.
points: Image: a read-only template of your app
Container: a running copy of an image
One image can start many containers

slides.heading: Dockerfile
slides.subtitle: The instructions for building an image.
points: FROM picks a base image
COPY adds your code
RUN installs dependencies
CMD sets the start command
examples: FROM node:20 for a Node.js app

slides.heading: Key commands
slides.subtitle: The four you'll use daily.
points: docker build -t app . builds an image
docker run -p 3000:3000 app starts it
docker ps lists running containers
docker compose up starts multi-container apps

title: REST API Design Best Practices
intro: A well-designed API is easy to guess, easy to use and hard to misuse. These conventions get you most of the way.

slides.heading: Use nouns
slides.subtitle: Resources in URLs, not actions.
points: GET /users, not GET /getUsers
Plural nouns for collections
Nest related data: /users/42/orders

slides.heading: HTTP methods
slides.subtitle: Let the method describe the action.
points: GET reads data
POST creates something new
PUT replaces, PATCH updates part of it
DELETE removes it

slides.heading: Status codes
slides.subtitle: Tell the client what happened.
points: 201 after creating a resource
400 for invalid input
404 when it doesn't exist
Never return 200 with an error inside

slides.heading: Version & paginate
slides.subtitle: Plan for growth from day one.
points: Version your API: /api/v1/
Paginate big lists: ?page=2&limit=20
Keep response shapes consistent

cta: What's the worst API design you've had to work with?

title: React Hooks Every Beginner Should Know
intro: Hooks let function components remember data and react to changes. These four cover most of what you'll write.

slides.heading: useState
slides.subtitle: Remember values between renders.
points: Returns the value and a setter function
Calling the setter re-renders the component
Use setX(prev => ...) for updates based on the old value

slides.heading: useEffect
slides.subtitle: Sync with things outside React.
points: Runs after the component renders
The dependency array controls when it re-runs
Return a cleanup function when needed

slides.heading: useRef
slides.subtitle: Keep a value without re-rendering.
points: Access DOM elements directly
Store values that survive re-renders
Changing .current doesn't re-render

slides.heading: useMemo & useCallback
slides.subtitle: Skip expensive work.
points: useMemo caches a computed value
useCallback caches a function
Add them when you notice real slowness

title: What Happens When You Type a URL
intro: Hitting Enter in your browser kicks off a surprisingly long chain of steps. Here's the journey, simplified.

slides.heading: 1. DNS Lookup
slides.subtitle: Turning a name into an IP address.
points: The browser asks DNS for the site's IP address
Answers are cached to speed up repeat visits

slides.heading: 2. Connecting
slides.subtitle: Opening a secure connection.
points: A TCP handshake connects to the server
A TLS handshake sets up HTTPS encryption
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP

slides.heading: 3. The Request
slides.subtitle: Asking the server for the page.
points: The browser sends a GET request with headers
The server replies with a status code and HTML
A CDN may answer instead of the origin server

slides.heading: 4. Rendering
slides.subtitle: Turning code into pixels.
points: HTML is parsed into the DOM
CSS is parsed into the CSSOM
Layout and paint draw the page
JavaScript can then update it

title: Terminal Commands Every Developer Uses
intro: You don't need to be a Linux expert. These commands cover most of your daily terminal work.

slides.heading: Navigation
slides.subtitle: Know where you are and move around.
points: pwd shows the current folder
ls -la lists files, including hidden ones
cd folder moves into a folder

slides.heading: Files & folders
slides.subtitle: Create, copy, move and delete.
points: mkdir name creates a folder
touch file creates an empty file
cp copies, mv moves or renames
rm deletes for good: there's no trash

slides.heading: Reading files
slides.subtitle: Look inside without an editor.
points: cat file prints a file
less file lets you scroll through it
tail -f file follows a log live
grep "text" file searches inside it

slides.heading: Processes
slides.subtitle: See and control what's running.
points: ps aux lists running processes
kill PID stops a process
chmod +x script.sh makes a script runnable
sudo runs a command as admin

title: Clean Code Habits That Save You Hours
intro: Code is read far more often than it's written. These habits make your code easier for everyone, including future you.

slides.heading: Meaningful names
slides.subtitle: Names should explain intent.
points: getUserById beats getData
Booleans read like questions: isActive
Avoid single letters outside short loops

slides.heading: Small functions
slides.subtitle: One function, one job.
points: If you need "and" to describe it, split it
Short functions are easier to test
And easier to reuse

slides.heading: DRY, carefully
slides.subtitle: Don't Repeat Yourself, within reason.
points: Extract logic you've copied several times
Don't merge code that only looks similar
A little duplication beats the wrong abstraction

slides.heading: Comments
slides.subtitle: Explain why, not what.
points: Good names remove most comments
Comment surprising decisions and workarounds
Delete commented-out code: git remembers it
